Exploratory Data Analysis

Leona Vracar

# Function for analysis of variables
variable_analysis <- function(vect) {
  result <- list(
    mean = mean(vect),
    median = median(vect),
    variance = var(vect),
    sd = sd(vect),
    IQR = IQR(vect),
    min = min(vect),
    max = max(vect),
    range = max(vect) - min(vect)
  )
  return(result)
}

# Format summary statistics as a table
# Execute this on a _result variable (output of variable_analysis(swiss$Fertility)) in a code block to get the  nice table in text)
print_nice <- function(result) {
  # Convert statistics to a formatted table
  table <- as.data.frame(t(as.data.frame(result)))
  colnames(table) <- "Value"  # value is 2nd column
  table <- round(table, 4)  
  
  # Print, left align and title
  knitr::kable(table, caption = "Summary Statistics", align = c("l", "r"))
}
# Function for 4 plots: box, histo, QQ, ECDF
plots_function <- function(input_vect, var_name = "default") {
  # mfrow sets 2x2 layout and mar sets plot margins
  par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1)) 
  
  #Boxplot
  boxplot(
    input_vect,
    main = paste("Boxplot of", var_name),
    col = "lightgreen",
    horizontal = TRUE 
  )
  
  # Histogram
  hist(
    input_vect,
    main = paste("Histogram of", var_name),
    xlab = var_name,
    col = "lightblue",
    freq = FALSE
  )
  lines(density(input_vect), col = "red", lwd = 2)  #density curve
  
  # Q-Q 
  qqnorm(
    input_vect,
    main = paste("Q-Q Plot of", var_name),
    col = "blue"
  )
  qqline(input_vect, col = "red", lwd = 2)  
  
  # ECDF
  plot(
    ecdf(input_vect),
    main = paste("ECDF of", var_name),
    xlab = var_name,
    ylab = "ECDF"
  )
  
  # Reset layout back to normal 1x1
  par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
}
# Function for outliers check using 1.5 × IQR 
calculate_outliers <- function(vect) {
  Q1 <- quantile(vect, 0.25)
  Q3 <- quantile(vect, 0.75)
  IQR <- Q3 - Q1
  result <- list(
    low_fence = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR,
    up_fence = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
  )
  return(result)
}
# function for scatterplot matrix
scatter_matrix <- function(data, main_title = "Scatterplot Matrix", point_color = "darkblue", point_size = 0.8) {
  pairs(
    data,
    main = main_title,
    col = point_color,
    cex = point_size
  )
}
# Function for correlation matrix
cor_matrix <- function(data) {
  # Compute cor matrix
  result <- cor(data, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
  # Print rounded matrix
  print(round(result, 2))
  
  # make heatmap with dendrogram/colors
  heatmap(
    result, 
    main = "Correlation Matrix", 
    col = colorRampPalette(c("blue", "white", "red"))(20)
  )
}

1 Swiss Socioeconomic Data

The dataset swiss contains 6 variables (columns) and 47 rows representing 47 French-spaking provinces of Switzerland at 1888.

The dataset provides information about socioeconomic indicators and fertility for each province.

head(swiss)

1.1 EDA of individual variables

In this section, we perform EDA on variables “Fertility”, “Agriculture”, “Education”, “Catholic” and “Infant Mortality”.

fertility_result <- variable_analysis(swiss$Fertility)
agriculture_result <- variable_analysis(swiss$Agriculture)
education_result <- variable_analysis(swiss$Education)
catholic_result <- variable_analysis(swiss$Catholic)
infant_result <- variable_analysis(swiss$Infant.Mortality)

1.1.1 Fertility

print_nice(fertility_result)
Summary Statistics
Value
mean 70.1426
median 70.4000
variance 156.0425
sd 12.4917
IQR 13.7500
min 35.0000
max 92.5000
range 57.5000

Location: The variable Fertility has a mean of 70.14 and a median of 70.4 suggesting that the data may be symmetric and that there are likely no (or just a few) outliers that skew the dateset (otherwise the mean as a non-robust measure would not so closely match the median).

Spread/variation: The data has a moderate spread with a SD of 12.49 which is small relative to the mean of 70.14 and overall range. The IQR is 13.75 which is small relative to the range is 12.49 suggesting that the middle 50% of the data points are in a narrow range around the median (also mean due to mean and median being almost identical).

# Call the function
plots_function(swiss$Fertility, var_name = "Fertility")

Boxplot: In the boxplot, we see two potential outliers that lie beyond the central ~95% of the data. However, these two points may not necessarily be outliers since the data is left-skewed (longer whiskers on the left and the location of the median in the left half of the box suggest this skew).

Histogram: From the histogram we clearly see the data is not symetrical, is left-skewed and unimodal with a single peak. This means that there are potential outliers in the left tail. Most of the data is concentrated around one SD above and below the mean (two largest bars are at 60-80).

Q-Q Plot: The left-skew caused by potential outliers is also visible in the Q-Q plot as there are data points deviating from the qqline (normal distribution) at the left end of the plot.

ECDF: The steep slope of the ECDF plot around 0.5 (which aligns with the median) also shows that most data-points are concentrated around this value. The curve has a left tail, again due to the two values outside the 95% of the data, one of which is the minimum value of the range at 35.

In the context of the dataset, it seems that fertility was mostly moderate to high with a few extremes in the lower end of the distribution that could be worth looking into, especially in correlation with other variables.

1.1.2.1 Extra: Shapiro-Wilks test to check normality

For the null hypothesis, we assume data is approximately normally distributed, while the alternative hypothesis is that data is not normally distributed.

shapiro.test(swiss$Agriculture)
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  swiss$Agriculture
## W = 0.96643, p-value = 0.193

With a p-value of 0.193, we do not reject the null hypothesis of normality; there is no strong evidence against a normal distribution.

1.1.3 Education

print_nice(education_result)
Summary Statistics

sd 9.6154
IQR 6.0000
min 1.0000

Location: The mean at 10.98 is above the median at 8 suggesting data points which are pulling the mean up from the central value.

Spread/Variation: The IQR tells us that 50% of data is in the range of IQR = 6. Such a tight IQR relative to the min (1) and max (53) values suggest that half the data is very tightly clustered. The SD of 9.62 is larger than the IQR meaning the SD is inflated by a few larger values.

Skewness: As stated, both the mean and SD (as non-robust measures) are inflated upwards compared to the median and IQR (their robust counterparts) which suggests a right skew or a few large outliers.

plots_function(swiss$Education, var_name = "Education")

Boxplot: The boxplot reflects the tight clustering of the data in the IQR (the box) as well as a right skew due to the longer right whisker and four outliers.

Histogram: From the density curve, the data looks bimodal with the first peak at the mean and a second one around 30.

Q-Q Plot: The higher values deviating from the qqline are also visible on the Q-Q plot. While we only identified 4 in the boxplot, there seem to be several more (6-7) visible in the Q-Q plot. The data does not follow a normal distribution.

ECDF: The ECDF is interesting as it shows a steep curve between ~1 and ~15 on the x-axis, with ~15 corresponding to 0.8 on the y-axis, meaning that ~80% of data is in this range (low variability). The long tails at ~20, ~30 and ~50 on the x-axis are extreme values causing the right-skew. In the context of the dataset, this means that most people (in 1888) had a low-level of education with just a few having higher levels. The max value of 53 matches the min value for agriculture and corresponds to the province “V. De Geneve” which likely had a more educated population due to being an urban center.

1.1.4 Catholic

print_nice(catholic_result)
Summary Statistics
Value
mean 41.1438

variance 1739.2945
sd 41.7049
IQR 87.9300
min 2.1500
max 100.0000

Location: The mean at 41.14 and median at 15.14 differ significantly which means the data is not symmetrical. Since the mean >> median, there are likely several extreme data points in the higher end of the distribution affecting the mean.

Spread/Variation: The IQR as a robust measure at 87.93 and the high SD as a non-robust one at 41.7 signify a broad distribution and highly variable data. This is further confirmed by broad range (97.85) between min at 2.15 and max at 100.

Skewness: The data is likely bimodal or right-skewed due to the mean being significantly higher than the median.

plots_function(swiss$Catholic, var_name = "Catholic")

Boxplot: The median is very close to the lower quartile (Q1) in the box meaning that most data points are likely in the lower range. There are no visual outliers but the distribution is very stretched out and the right whisker together with the position of the median suggest a right skew.

Histogram: The histogram has 2 peaks i.e. a bimodal distribution. Very few values are in the central part of the range (between 30 and 70). The density curve may be a bit misleading because it doesn’t show the sharp peaks visible in the bars.

Q-Q Plot: The data is clearly bimodal. The tail in the low end (negative quantiles on the x-axis) is below the normalcy line which suggests smaller values compared to a normal distribution. Most data points are in this lower end with the median (at 0 quantile on the x-axis) being significantly below the expected median value for a normal distribution. The higher end of the data (between ~0.5-2 quantiles on x-axis) show the higher end of the bimodal distribution.

ECDF: This plot confirms that the data is bimodal with most values (~0.6 on y-axis or 60%) being in a narrow lower range, a few dispersed values in the mid-range and another distinct peak (~0.75 on y-axis or at 75%) in the high range.

In the context of the dataset, the bimodal distribution means that most provinces were either completely non-Catholic or close to 100% Catholic. However, we do not have the data about the population size of each province so we cannot make any statements about the the absolute number of Christians or non-Christians per province. For example, the max value of 100 corresponding to the province Herens makes it seem like 100% of the inhabitants are Christian but there may only be a very small population living in this province.

1.2 Correlation between variables

Scatterplot Matrix

# Selecting variables (making a subset of those that we're interested in)
swiss_subset <- swiss[, c("Fertility", "Agriculture", "Education", "Catholic", "Infant.Mortality")]

# Scatterplot matrix
scatter_matrix(swiss_subset)

The scatterplot matrix shows visible patterns between some variables:

  1. Fertility and Agriculture seem to have a positive correlation.
  2. Fertility and Education seem to have a negative correlation.
  3. Infant mortality and Fertility seem to have a positive correlation.
  4. Agriculture and Education seem to have a negative correlation.

To examine these correlations further, we look at a correlation matrix in the next step.

Correlation Matrix

cor_matrix(swiss_subset)
##                  Fertility Agriculture Education Catholic Infant.Mortality
## Fertility             1.00        0.35     -0.66     0.46             0.42
## Agriculture           0.35        1.00     -0.64     0.40            -0.06
## Education            -0.66       -0.64      1.00    -0.15            -0.10
## Catholic              0.46        0.40     -0.15     1.00             0.18
## Infant.Mortality      0.42       -0.06     -0.10     0.18             1.00

The correlation matrix confirms the correlations we already identified and additionally shows a positive correlation between Fertility and Catholic (r = 0.46).

Some possible conclusions from the correlations are:

Fertility, Agriculture and Education: Swiss provinces with higher rates of agricultural activity had a higher fertility rate while education and fertility were negatively correlated (r = -0.66). In addition, education and agriculture were strongly negatively correlated (r = -0.64), suggesting that education levels were lower in rural areas and higher in urban areas. These findings are in line with common demographic patterns where lower birth rates are associated with higher education levels.

Fertility and Infant Mortality: Fertility and infant mortality are positively correlated (r = 0.46). This association may reflect underlying socioeconomic or geographic differences between provinces; the observational data do not establish a causal relationship.

Catholic: One somewhat peculiar finding was the positive correlation between Catholic and Fertility (r = 0.46) suggesting that Catholic provinces had higher fertility rates. Catholicism rates also had a positive correlation with Agriculture (r = 0.40) suggesting that more agricultural communities were more religious and had a higher rate of fertility.

2.1 EDA of individual variables

This section explores the variables “Population”, “Income”, “Illiteracy”, “Life.Exp”, “Murder”, “HS Grade” and “Frost”.

pop_result <- variable_analysis(state.x77_dataframe$Population)
inc_result <- variable_analysis(state.x77_dataframe$Income)
illi_result <- variable_analysis(state.x77_dataframe$Illiteracy)
life_exp_result <- variable_analysis(state.x77_dataframe$`Life Exp`)
murder_result <- variable_analysis(state.x77_dataframe$Murder)
hs_grad_result <- variable_analysis(state.x77_dataframe$`HS Grad`)
frost_result <- variable_analysis(state.x77_dataframe$Frost)

2.1.1 Population

print_nice(pop_result)
Summary Statistics
Value
mean 4246.420
median 2838.500
variance 19931683.759
sd 4464.491
IQR 3889.000
min 365.000
max 21198.000

Location: The mean at 4246.42 and median at 2838.5 diverge significantly which suggests the data is not symmetrical. Median is robust and hence appropriate as the locus for this dataset.

Spread: The data has a high variance 1.9931684^{7} and standard deviation 4464.49 which means the population numbers are widely different across states. The IQR of 3889 means that the middle 50% of states have populations in this range.

Skewness: The data is skewed to the right since mean >> median.

plots_function(state.x77_dataframe$Population, var_name = "Population")

Boxplot: Outliers are visible beyond the right whisker, 3 potential outliers and 2 definite ones. The elongated right whisker also suggests a right skew.

Histogram: The right-skew is clearly visible in the histogram. Most states have a population up to 7000, while there are a few ones with larger population numbers between 10 000 and 25 000. It could be argued that the data is unimodal with several outliers or the outliers could be grouped together in a cluster in a bimodal dataset since population is (unsurprisingly) higher in more urban states like California and New York.

Q-Q Plot: The dataset deviates from a normal distribution, especially at the upper end. Again, the deviation is caused by the outliers.

ECDF: The ECDF plot shows a steep rise in the beginning, meaning many states have low populations. The more elongated points at the right of the plot are the few states with large populations.

Location: Both the mean at 1.17 and the median at 0.95 are low and pretty close together without any outliers. While the mean is appropriate here as a measure of central tendency, it is slightly higher than the median, potentially indicating a slight right-skew.

The Q-Q plot shows significant deviations from normality beyond 10 on the y-axis (sample quantlies) which corresponds to the second peak in the bimodal distribution.

In the context of the dataset, murder rates seem to be surprisingly high in some states compared to the rest of the country.

plots_function(state.x77_dataframe$`HS Grad`, var_name = "HS Grad")

Histogram: The histogram reveals two peaks: a smaller one in the lower range and a larger peak in the higher range. This means that the percentage of high school graduates in most states is between ~50-60%. However, a smaller but non-negligible number of states have lower high school graduation rates in the ~38-43% range.

Q-Q Plot and ECDF: The Q-Q plot shows that the data strongly deviates from a normal distribution, especially in the lower range which corresponds to the first mode. The ECDF illustrates the separation of the two peaks: a short but steep curve of the first mode is followed by a plateau between ~43 and ~46 on the x-axis, followed by a second curve with a more gradual increase but a small steep rise at ~53. The small steep rise at ~53 on the ECDF curve signifies that there is a concentration of data at this point which may be part of the reason why the mean also has this value and wasn’t displaced from the median by the bimodal distribution.

range 188.0000

Location: The mean (104.46) and (114.5) differ by 10 days which suggests that there are low values displacing the mean below the median. The mean approximates the central tendency of the data but the median is more reliable as the locus in this case.

Spread: The standard deviation (51.98) is large relative to the overall range of the data (188), meaning that the data is highly spread out and variable.

Skewness: From the histogram and Q-Q plot we can conclude that the data is actually bimodal with some states having low numbers of days with freezing temperatures (e.g. Hawaii, our min value of 0).

plots_function(state.x77_dataframe$Frost, var_name = "Frost")

Boxplot: The boxplot is not a useful visualization for this data as it does not show the bimodal distribution. The only useful information we can deduce is that the slightly longer left whisker means there are several states with little to no days with below-freezing temperatures.

Histogram: The density curve is misleading as it smooths out the first peak of the bimodal distribution i.e. the data contained in the first bar. However the histogram bars are the best visualization here for the bimodallity of the data.

Q-Q Plot: The Q-Q plot on its own it would not clearly indicate bimodality as most points fall close to the red qqline. However, the typical S-shaped curve of a bimodal distribution is still visible in the Q-Q plot, albeit its S-shape is more flattened out and may be difficult to notice at first glance.

ECDF: Similarly, the ECDF plot barely makes the bimodal distribution visible. It is possible to identify a clear second mode around 130 on the x-axis but the first mode is barely distinguishable between 5 and 10.

2.2 Correlation between variables

2.2.1 Scatterplot Matrix

usa_subset <- state.x77[, c("Population", "Income", "Illiteracy", "Life Exp", 
                            "Murder", "HS Grad", "Frost")]
# Scatterplot matrix
scatter_matrix(usa_subset)

2.2.2 Correlation Matrix

cor_matrix(usa_subset)
##            Population Income Illiteracy Life Exp Murder HS Grad Frost
## Population       1.00   0.21       0.11    -0.07   0.34   -0.10 -0.33
## Income           0.21   1.00      -0.44     0.34  -0.23    0.62  0.23
## Illiteracy       0.11  -0.44       1.00    -0.59   0.70   -0.66 -0.67
## Life Exp        -0.07   0.34      -0.59     1.00  -0.78    0.58  0.26
## Murder           0.34  -0.23       0.70    -0.78   1.00   -0.49 -0.54
## HS Grad         -0.10   0.62      -0.66     0.58  -0.49    1.00  0.37
## Frost           -0.33   0.23      -0.67     0.26  -0.54    0.37  1.00

In this part, we look at some interesting correlations between the variables:

Illiteracy and Murder Rate (0.70): A strong positive correlation suggests that states with higher illiteracy rates tend to have higher murder rates. This relationship should not be interpreted causally.

Illiteracy and Life Expectancy (-0.59): The negative correlation implies that states with higher illiteracy rates tend to have lower life expectancy. We can speculate that illiteracy likely doesn’t exist in isolation but that it is the result of generally worse economic conditions and less access to things such as healthcare, balanced food or even free time to learn to read and write. Hence, illiteracy probably doesn’t lower life expectancy on its own but it signifies a larger issue like poverty in these states which leads to lower life expectancy and more crime.

Murder Rate and Life Expectancy (-0.78): A strong negative correlation indicates that states with higher murder rates have lower life expectancy, which is not surprising and maybe shows that there are public safety issues in these states.

HS Graduation Rate and Life Expectancy (0.58): A positive correlation suggests that states with higher high school graduation rates also tend to have longer life expectancy. Again, we cannot make the conclusion that graduating high school increases life expectancy but the positive correlation may point to other societal issues which cause people to not graduate high school such as worse living conditions which in turn may lower life expectancy.

Income and HS Graduation Rate (0.62): A moderately strong positive correlation suggests that states with higher average income levels tend to have higher high school graduation rates, which makes sense as richer states may have more funding for education, more people can afford education and access it more easily.

Frost and Murder Rate (-0.54): A negative correlation suggests that colder states (those with more frost days) tend to have lower murder rates.

Population and Murder Rate (0.34): A weak positive correlation suggests that more populous states tend to have slightly higher murder rates maybe because crime is often concentrated in big cities.

3 Lake Huron Time-Series Data

The dataset LakeHuron contains annual measurements of the level of Lake Huron 1875-1972 (in feet).

LakeHuron <- LakeHuron

3.1 EDA of lake levels

3.1.1 Lake levels without considering the time aspect

# To analyze just the lake levels we convert them to a numeric vector
# LakeHuron is a ts object in R
lake_levels <- as.numeric(LakeHuron)

levels_result <- variable_analysis(lake_levels)
print_nice(levels_result)

IQR 1.7400
min 575.9600

Location: The mean (579) and median (579.12) are close to being identical which suggests a high level of symmetry and no outliers or extreme values.

Spread: The data has a moderate range (5.9) and moderate spread. The middle 50% of data is also pretty concentrated with an IQR of 1.74.

Skewness: The mean is slightly lower than the median which suggests that a few values below the median may be causing a slight deviation from symmetry. However, the data still appears to be very close to perfect symmetry.

plots_function(lake_levels, var_name = "Lake Levels (no time)")

Boxplot: A few more data points below the median (the black line) can be deduced from the boxplot. Besides this, the data seems symmetric with no outliers.

Histogram: Data is approximately symmetric and unimodal with a very slight left tail but not nearly enough to identify skewness.

Q-Q Plot: Data is normally distributed with just a few deviations from the red qqline at the extremes.

ECDF: The ECDF is smooth and continuous, indicating no outliers.

3.1.2 Lake levels including the time aspect

From the time series plot above, there seems to be a decline in water levels as time progresses. However, we can’t say if this decline is significant at this stage of analysis.

Another interesting element in this data is that the max value was recorded in the first few years of measurements while the lowest water level was recorded near the end around 1965.

plot(LakeHuron, main = "Lake Huron Water Levels (1875–1972)",
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Water Level", col = "blue", type = "l", xaxt = "n")
axis(1, at = seq(1875, 1975, by = 5), labels = seq(1875, 1975, by = 5))

# Min and max values
points(time(LakeHuron)[which.min(LakeHuron)], levels_result$min, col = "red", pch = 19)
points(time(LakeHuron)[which.max(LakeHuron)], levels_result$max, col = "red", pch = 19)

Upon examining the lowest recorded values (the valleys on the plot), it appears that over time the lowest recorded water level was being pushed further and further down.

4.3 Simpson’s paradox & Interpretation

Simpson’s Paradox is a statistical phenomenon that occurs when subgroups are combined into one group. The process of aggregating data can cause the apparent direction and strength of the relationship between two variables to change.

In the case of our Titanic dataset one would think that the survival rate of the female crew was very low. But if we look at the “Sex vs. Survived” plot in general the females had a better survival outcome. This is because there were not many female crew members, but overall 20 out of 23 female crew members survived.

Furthermore if we only look at “Class vs. Survived” one could think, that the survival is independent from sex - so the the better the class, the better the survival outcome. But if we also include the sex, we see for example that the survival rate of females in the first class is almost 100%, whereas men in the first class only had a survival rate of about 34%.

Then if we look closely at the “Children in the Age vs. Survived” plot, we may think children do have a higher survival rate than adults. If we also include the class it becomes clear, that the survival rate of children is also very dependent on the class. The higher the class, the higher the survival rates in children.
